newsitem.title: CANADA: Goodale sees barley vote by end February 1997.
newsitem.headline: Goodale sees barley vote by end February 1997.

text.p: Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale on Friday said a farmers' vote on the Canadian Wheat Board's monopoly over barley exports will take place no later than the end of February 1997.

"I'm anxious to make sure the vote gets done early enough that it doesn't interfere with farmers spring seeding activity and if you lapse into March, you're getting pretty close," Goodale said outside a Canada Grains Council conference.
The CWB's barley export monopoly was criticized last year when spot prices at U.S. border elevators exceeded its offers.
Prairie farmers who can prove they grew barley in the last five years will be eligible to vote by mail-in ballot.
They will be asked to choose between these two options:
Open Market Option: Remove all barley from the CWB and place it entirely on the open market for all domestic and export sales, or-
Single-Seller Option: Maintain the CWB as the single-desk seller for all barley with the continuing exception of feed barley sold domestically.
The CWB held an 11 percent share of the world feed barley market in 1994/95 (Aug/July), exporting 30 percent of output.
It held a 48 percent share of the world malting barley market in that same period, CWB figures show.
"An independent firm of expert professionals will handle all of the administration of the vote to ensure fairness and accuracy," Goodale said.
To some in the industry, the questions have become a point of controversy.
"Australia has voluntary barley pooling. You're asking the wrong question, voluntary pooling does work," United Grain Growers Ltd Ken Motiuk said to Goodale.
"I certainly respect those who hold that point of view, but I don't think it's as clear cut as that," Goodale said.
Campaign spending limits by parties for or against the questions were not likely to be imposed.
"I would prefer to avoid spending limits if at all possible...that kind of regulation would be extremely difficult to administer," he added.
Legislation to revamp the CWB's structure from government-appointed commissioners to a farmer-elected board of directors should go before Parliament shortly, he said.
One or two of the 11 to 15 proposed directors would be government officials. Others may include non-agricultural business leaders with the majority of the board made up of producers, Goodale said.
